plain_english: "But what," our opponent asks, "stops us from combining virtue and pleasure? Why can't we create the highest good by mixing honor and pleasure together?" Here's why: only honorable things can be part of honor. The highest good would lose its purity if it contained anything unlike its best part. Even the joy that comes from virtue — though it's a good thing — isn't part of the absolute good. Neither are cheerfulness or peace of mind. These are good things, but they just follow from the highest good. They don't make it more perfect, even though they come from the noblest causes.
original_excerpt: "But what," asks our adversary, "is there to hinder virtue and pleasure being combined together, and a highest good being thus formed, so that honour and pleasure may be the same thing?" Because nothing except what is honourable can form a part of honour, and the highest good would lose its purity if it were to see within itself anything unlike its own better part. Even the joy which arises from virtue, although it be a good thing, yet is not a part of absolute good, any more than cheerfulness or peace of mind, which are indeed good things, but which merely follow the highest good, and do not contribute to its perfection, although they are generated by the noblest causes.

plain_english: But anyone who tries to combine virtue with pleasure — and it's always a one-sided alliance — weakens virtue by mixing it with something weak. This puts freedom under the yoke. Freedom can only stay unconquered when it values nothing more than itself. Once you need pleasure, you start needing Fortune's help. And that's complete slavery. Your life becomes anxious, suspicious, timid, afraid of setbacks. You live in agony waiting for crucial moments. You can't give virtue a solid foundation if you tell it to stand on something shaky. And what could be shakier than depending on chance and the ups and downs of the body and everything that affects the body?
original_excerpt: Whoever on the other hand forms an alliance, and that, too, a one-sided one, between virtue and pleasure, clogs whatever strength the one may possess by the weakness of the other, and sends liberty under the yoke, for liberty can only remain unconquered as long as she knows nothing more valuable than herself: for he begins to need the help of Fortune, which is the most utter slavery: his life becomes anxious, full of suspicion, timorous, fearful of accidents, waiting in agony for critical moments of time. You do not afford virtue a solid immoveable base if you bid it stand on what is unsteady: and what can be so unsteady as dependence on mere chance, and the vicissitudes of the body and of those things which act on the body?

plain_english: How can a man serve God and accept whatever happens with a cheerful heart? How can he never complain about his fate and see the good in everything that befalls him if he gets upset by tiny pleasures and pains? A man can't protect his country well, or fight for justice, or defend his friends if he's always chasing after pleasures.
original_excerpt: How can such a man obey God and receive everything which comes to pass in a cheerful spirit, never complaining of fate, and putting a good construction upon everything that befalls him, if he be agitated by the petty pin-pricks of pleasures and pains? A man cannot be a good protector of his country, a good avenger of her wrongs, or a good defender of his friends, if he be inclined to pleasures.

plain_english: Let the highest good rise to a place where nothing can knock it down. A place where pain cannot reach, where hope and fear cannot touch it, where nothing can weaken what makes it the "highest good." Only virtue can reach that high ground. She must help us climb that hill. Once there, virtue will stand firm and face whatever comes — not just with resignation, but willingly. She knows that hard times follow natural laws. Like a good soldier, she will bear her wounds and count her scars. Even when pierced through and dying, she will still love the general she dies for. She will remember the old saying: "Follow God."
original_excerpt: Let the highest good, then, rise to that height from whence no force can dislodge it, whither neither pain can ascend, nor hope, nor fear, nor anything else that can impair the authority of the "highest good." Thither virtue alone can make her way: by her aid that hill must be climbed: she will bravely stand her ground and endure whatever may befal her not only resignedly, but even willingly: she will know that all hard times come in obedience to natural laws, and like a good soldier she will bear wounds, count scars, and when transfixed and dying will yet adore the general for whom she falls: she will bear in mind the old maxim "Follow God."

plain_english: On the other hand, someone who grumbles and complains and feels sorry for himself is still forced to obey fate's orders. He gets dragged along to do what must be done, no matter how much he fights it. But what madness is it to be dragged rather than to go willingly? It's just as crazy, I swear, as it is foolish and ignorant to grieve because you didn't get something you wanted, or because something treated you harshly. It's equally foolish to be surprised or angry at the troubles that hit good people and bad people alike — I mean sickness, death, illness, and all the other painful accidents of human life.
original_excerpt: On the other hand, he who grumbles and complains and bemoans himself is nevertheless forcibly obliged to obey orders, and is dragged away, however much against his will, to carry them out: yet what madness is it to be dragged rather than to follow? as great, by Hercules, as it is folly and ignorance of one's true position to grieve because one has not got something or because something has caused us rough treatment, or to be surprised or indignant at those ills which befall good men as well as bad ones, I mean diseases, deaths, illnesses, and the other cross accidents of human life.

plain_english: Let us accept with courage whatever the universe requires us to endure. We are all bound by the same promise: to bear the troubles of human life and submit gracefully to what we cannot change. We were born into a kingdom where God rules. Our freedom comes from obeying God.
original_excerpt: Let us bear with magnanimity whatever the system of the universe makes it needful for us to bear: we are all bound by this oath: "To bear the ills of mortal life, and to submit with a good grace to what we cannot avoid." We have been born into a monarchy: our liberty is to obey God.
